$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(0,0,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,0,0⟩ \\ ⟨\sqrt{3}t,\,{t}^{2},\,{t}^{3}⟩ & =⟨0,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}t=0 \\ {t}^{2}=0 \\ {t}^{3}=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(0,0,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{3},\,2t,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨\sqrt{3},\,2(0),\,3({0}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{3},0,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3+0+0} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,6t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨0,\,2,\,6(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \sqrt{3} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(2\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-af4cee66-027d-5ab7-8663-bfb226292ce7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $r(t)=⟨\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3},{t}^{2},\,\,t⟩$ for $t>0$, use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(\frac{2}{3},1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(\frac{2}{3},1,1)$ on the given curve. We know that 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨\frac{2}{3},1,1⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3},{t}^{2},\,\,t⟩ & =⟨\frac{2}{3},1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}=\frac{2}{3} \\ {t}^{2}=1 \\ t=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(\frac{2}{3},1,1)$ is at the tip of $r(1).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(1),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},\,2t,\,1⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨2,2,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨4t,\,2,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨4,2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-2i+4j-4k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{3}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d1859a39-a2db-5a73-b35c-f7fe6ddee607"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d1859a39-a2db-5a73-b35c-f7fe6ddee607" :answer-field/id #uuid "d1859a39-a2db-5a73-b35c-f7fe6ddee607" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1b297cdb-aecf-5f48-af66-84c29ddda497" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b1a80722-6c7c-5c77-acb3-2b2fa7e23bbb" "answer-1b297cdb-aecf-5f48-af66-84c29ddda497" "answer-123d29d6-8aaf-5afb-862b-e46ce76281e2" "answer-2f0e8910-4151-5310-9c16-3f2d1d8be9a0" "answer-2bc57f81-b019-581e-9c4a-3f95a1c41bbd"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b1a80722-6c7c-5c77-acb3-2b2fa7e23bbb" :answer/id #uuid "b1a80722-6c7c-5c77-acb3-2b2fa7e23bbb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{27}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1b297cdb-aecf-5f48-af66-84c29ddda497" :answer/id #uuid "1b297cdb-aecf-5f48-af66-84c29ddda497" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{9}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-123d29d6-8aaf-5afb-862b-e46ce76281e2" :answer/id #uuid "123d29d6-8aaf-5afb-862b-e46ce76281e2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{8}{27}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2f0e8910-4151-5310-9c16-3f2d1d8be9a0" :answer/id #uuid "2f0e8910-4151-5310-9c16-3f2d1d8be9a0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{27}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2bc57f81-b019-581e-9c4a-3f95a1c41bbd" :answer/id #uuid "2bc57f81-b019-581e-9c4a-3f95a1c41bbd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{9}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351507 :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(2,1,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2,1,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t,\,{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩ & =⟨2,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2t=2 \\ {t}^{2}=1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,1,0)$ is at the tip of $r(1).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(1),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2t,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨2,2,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4i+2j+4k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+4+16} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{3}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-de097a4f-c54e-5f8e-b869-e4dc2af58fad" :question/id #uuid "de097a4f-c54e-5f8e-b869-e4dc2af58fad" :question/math-academy-id "q-83407" :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{2t},\,2t⟩,$ use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(1,1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(1,1,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨1,1,0⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{2t},\,2t⟩ & =⟨1,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}=1 \\ {e}^{2t}=1 \\ 2t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,1,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{2t},\,2⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨1,2,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{2t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,4{e}^{2t},\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨1,4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-8i+2j+2k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{(-8)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}}=\frac{6\sqrt{2}}{{3}^{3}}=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-998024b6-f7ae-51f5-8648-5d3da46e7c95"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-998024b6-f7ae-51f5-8648-5d3da46e7c95" :answer-field/id #uuid "998024b6-f7ae-51f5-8648-5d3da46e7c95" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-77770b63-6e34-588d-bcf9-716fc7c40db7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-77770b63-6e34-588d-bcf9-716fc7c40db7" "answer-33ab4b89-4470-5e8b-aee7-5a0fe5da5f2f" "answer-54fa053c-1b85-5eca-ba73-3ffa7456b013" "answer-fc8a20ec-0cfe-5f28-9075-f6395f297291" "answer-26a6f877-facd-5ea0-8579-e0d7c191bd3a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-77770b63-6e34-588d-bcf9-716fc7c40db7" :answer/id #uuid "77770b63-6e34-588d-bcf9-716fc7c40db7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{9}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-33ab4b89-4470-5e8b-aee7-5a0fe5da5f2f" :answer/id #uuid "33ab4b89-4470-5e8b-aee7-5a0fe5da5f2f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{9}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-54fa053c-1b85-5eca-ba73-3ffa7456b013" :answer/id #uuid "54fa053c-1b85-5eca-ba73-3ffa7456b013" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fc8a20ec-0cfe-5f28-9075-f6395f297291" :answer/id #uuid "fc8a20ec-0cfe-5f28-9075-f6395f297291" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-26a6f877-facd-5ea0-8579-e0d7c191bd3a" :answer/id #uuid "26a6f877-facd-5ea0-8579-e0d7c191bd3a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186266124 :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(0,-3,4\pi )$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,-3,4\pi ⟩ \\ ⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4t⟩ & =⟨0,-3,4\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t=0 \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t=-3 \\ 4t=4\pi .\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=\pi .$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(0,-3,4\pi )$ is at the tip of $r(\pi ).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,4⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,0,4⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,3,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -3 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-12i-9k \\  & =3(-4i-3k) \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =3\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{16+9} \\  & =3(5) \\  & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6-3{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2)⟩=⟨-6t,\,0,\,6⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-6t)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+36} \\  & =\sqrt{36({t}^{2}+1)} \\  & =6\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative ${r}^{″}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-6t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6)⟩=⟨-6,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨-6t,0,6⟩\times ⟨-6,0,0⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -6t & 0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-6t & 6 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-6t & 0 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-36\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =36\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{36}{{(6\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1})}^{3}}=\frac{1}{6({t}^{2}+1)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d4649305-d5dc-5854-97b6-ea90ae323c38"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨t,\,\sqrt{t}⟩$ as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4t}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4t+1}{4t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{4t+1}}{2\sqrt{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}},\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}} & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} &  \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}})}{{(\frac{\sqrt{4t+1}}{2\sqrt{t}})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}})}{(\frac{\sqrt{(4t+1)^{3}}}{8\sqrt{{t}^{3}}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{(4t+1)^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-afb164f4-0f92-5e1b-9127-b2a957f405bf"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2cos)^{2}+(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}=\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩=⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -3\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =(-6{cos}^{2}⁡t-6{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-6\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=6.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6}{(\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{sin}^{2}⁡t})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6}{(4{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{sin}^{2}⁡t)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9607fc20-f180-54be-8b8c-9a4822e7bd6e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121136 :tutorial/content "Recall that if the curve $\mathbf r(s)$ is parametrized by arc length $s,$ then the curvature of $\mathbf{r}$ is defined as

$$
\kappa(s) =  \left\| \dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf T}{\textrm{d}s}  \right\|.
$$

Moreover, if $\mathbf r(t)$ is parametrized by a general parameter $t,$ we have the following formula for the curvature:

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}
$$

where $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}$ is the unit tangent vector to the curve. 

It can be shown that the curvature of $\mathbf r(t)$ can also be found using the following cross product formula:

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}
$$

We'll derive this formula at the end of the lesson. For now, let's get some practice at applying it." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121137 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a plane curve $C$ that is parametrized by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle x(t), \: y(t) \rangle.
$$

At first glance, it looks as though the cross product curvature formula cannot be applied since cross products apply to three-dimensional vectors, whereas the given vector $\mathbf{r}(t)$ has only two dimensions.

However, this curve can also be viewed as a curve in three-dimensional space that lies on the plane $z=0.$ In this case, $\mathbf{r}(t)$ can be considered as a vector-valued function with $z$-component equal to zero:

$$
\mathbf r(t)= \langle x(t), \: y(t), \: 0 \rangle
$$

As a result, the curvature $\kappa$ of our plane curve $C$ can be calculated using our cross product formula:

$$
\kappa(t)=\dfrac{\|{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)}\times {\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime}(t)}\|}{\|{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)}\|^3}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121138 :tutorial/content "Recall that if the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ is parametrized by a general parameter $t,$ then the curvature of $\mathbf{r}$ is given by

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|},
$$

where $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}$ is the unit tangent vector to the curve. 

Here, $\mathbf r'(t)$ is a vector function and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|$ is a scalar function.
So, we differentiate $\mathbf T(t)$ by using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(T) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{′}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}({r}^{′}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{″}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the cross product of a vector with itself equals $\mathbf{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\times {T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\times (\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{″}(t)) \\  & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,({r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the magnitude of both sides and use the fact that $\mathbf T$ is a unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖T(t)\times {T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ ‖T(t)‖\cdot ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ 1\cdot ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|} = \dfrac{\left\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \right\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186120035 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(0,0,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,0,0⟩ \\ ⟨\sqrt{3}t,\,{t}^{2},\,{t}^{3}⟩ & =⟨0,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}t=0 \\ {t}^{2}=0 \\ {t}^{3}=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(0,0,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{3},\,2t,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨\sqrt{3},\,2(0),\,3({0}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{3},0,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3+0+0} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,6t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨0,\,2,\,6(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \sqrt{3} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(2\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-af4cee66-027d-5ab7-8663-bfb226292ce7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $r(t)=⟨\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3},{t}^{2},\,\,t⟩$ for $t>0$, use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(\frac{2}{3},1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(\frac{2}{3},1,1)$ on the given curve. We know that 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨\frac{2}{3},1,1⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3},{t}^{2},\,\,t⟩ & =⟨\frac{2}{3},1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}=\frac{2}{3} \\ {t}^{2}=1 \\ t=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(\frac{2}{3},1,1)$ is at the tip of $r(1).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(1),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},\,2t,\,1⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨2,2,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨4t,\,2,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨4,2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-2i+4j-4k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+4k.$*" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are told that

$$
{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+4k,
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(4)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+16} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{(\sqrt{5})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2840ac15-6a7c-5a69-ab78-2aa96a22daa0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id curvature of the curve $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩$, as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)⟩=⟨8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}+(-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}}=\sqrt{100{cos}^{2}⁡2t}=10|\operatorname{cos}⁡2t|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨8\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),-6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩=⟨-16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,0⟩\times ⟨-16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & -6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & 0 \\ -16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t & 12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & -6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ -16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t & 12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =(96\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-96\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,k \\  & =0\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=0.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{0}{(10|\operatorname{cos}⁡2t|)^{3}}=0.\end{aligned}

formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨t,\,\sqrt{t}⟩$ as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4t}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4t+1}{4t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{4t+1}}{2\sqrt{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}},\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}} & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} &  \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}})}{{(\frac{\sqrt{4t+1}}{2\sqrt{t}})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}})}{(\frac{\sqrt{(4t+1)^{3}}}{8\sqrt{{t}^{3}}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{(4t+1)^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-afb164f4-0f92-5e1b-9127-b2a957f405bf"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2cos)^{2}+(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}=\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩=⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -3\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =(-6{cos}^{2}⁡t-6{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-6\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=6.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6}{(\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{sin}^{2}⁡t})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6}{(4{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{sin}^{2}⁡t)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}

:db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121136 :tutorial/content "Recall that if the curve $\mathbf r(s)$ is parametrized by arc length $s,$ then the curvature of $\mathbf{r}$ is defined as

$$
\kappa(s) =  \left\| \dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf T}{\textrm{d}s}  \right\|.
$$

Moreover, if $\mathbf r(t)$ is parametrized by a general parameter $t,$ we have the following formula for the curvature:

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}
$$

where $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}$ is the unit tangent vector to the curve. 

It can be shown that the curvature of $\mathbf r(t)$ can also be found using the following cross product formula:

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}
$$

We'll derive this formula at the end of the lesson. For now, let's get some practice at applying it." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121137 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a plane curve $C$ that is parametrized by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle x(t), \: y(t) \rangle.
$$

At first glance, it looks as though the cross product curvature formula cannot be applied since cross products apply to three-dimensional vectors, whereas the given vector $\mathbf{r}(t)$ has only two dimensions.

However, this curve can also be viewed as a curve in three-dimensional space that lies on the plane $z=0.$ In this case, $\mathbf{r}(t)$ can be considered as a vector-valued function with $z$-component equal to zero:

$$
\mathbf r(t)= \langle x(t), \: y(t), \: 0 \rangle
$$

As a result, the curvature $\kappa$ of our plane curve $C$ can be calculated using our cross product formula:

$$
\kappa(t)=\dfrac{\|{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)}\times {\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime}(t)}\|}{\|{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)}\|^3}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121138 :tutorial/content "Recall that if the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ is parametrized by a general parameter $t,$ then the curvature of $\mathbf{r}$ is given by

\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|},
$$

where $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}$ is the unit tangent vector to the curve. 

Here, $\mathbf r'(t)$ is a vector function and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|$ is a scalar function.
So, we differentiate $\mathbf T(t)$ by using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(T) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{′}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}({r}^{′}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{″}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the cross product of a vector with itself equals $\mathbf{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\times {T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\times (\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{″}(t)) \\  & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,({r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the magnitude of both sides and use the fact that $\mathbf T$ is a unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖T(t)\times {T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ ‖T(t)‖\cdot ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ 1\cdot ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|} = \dfrac{\left\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \right\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186120035 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-449eabe4-56aa-5632-8405-aab3edd3f407" :question/id #uuid "449eabe4-56aa-5632-8405-aab3edd3f407"] ["question-449eabe4-56aa-5632-8405-aab3edd3f407" :question/math-academy-id "q-131973"] ["question-449eabe4-56aa-5632-8405-aab3edd3f407" :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\sqrt{3}t,\,{t}^{2},\,{t}^{3}⟩$ for $t\ge 0,$ use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(0,0,0).$"] ["question-449eabe4-56aa-5632-8405-aab3edd3f407" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

["question-e89f4c3b-6723-58b1-b21d-dbb9b8ced775" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(\frac{2}{3},1,1)$ on the given curve. We know that 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨\frac{2}{3},1,1⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3},{t}^{2},\,\,t⟩ & =⟨\frac{2}{3},1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}=\frac{2}{3} \\ {t}^{2}=1 \\ t=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(\frac{2}{3},1,1)$ is at the tip of $r(1).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(1),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖:$

$$

$$

$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-2i+4j-4k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨8\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),-6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩=⟨-16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,0⟩\times ⟨-16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & -6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & 0 \\ -16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t & 12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & -6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ -16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t & 12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =(96\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-96\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,k \\  & =0\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=0.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{0}{(10|\operatorname{cos}⁡2t|)^{3}}=0.\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4t}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4t+1}{4t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{4t+1}}{2\sqrt{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}},\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}} & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} &  \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}})}{{(\frac{\sqrt{4t+1}}{2\sqrt{t}})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}})}{(\frac{\sqrt{(4t+1)^{3}}}{8\sqrt{{t}^{3}}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{(4t+1)^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-076128a8-7495-5bb6-b7b4-2c35cb671771" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-afb164f4-0f92-5e1b-9127-b2a957f405bf" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $\mathbf r(t) = \langle t, -2t, t^2 \rangle$ at the point where $t = 1.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the curvature $\kappa (t),$ we will use the following formula:

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t),$ $\mathbf r'(1),$ and $\|\mathbf r'(1)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2,\,2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1,-2,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find $\mathbf r''(t)$ and $\mathbf r''(1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2),2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0,2⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,0,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4\,i-2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{20} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}}=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{{3}^{3}}=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049132} {:db/id 17592186049196} {:db/id 17592186120325 :question/id #uuid "edf1c08a-3bb6-585d-ba64-51f403188220" :question/math-academy-id "q-34335"} {:db/id 17592186120496 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4t⟩$ for $0\le t<2\pi ,$ use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(0,-3,4\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(0,-3,4\pi )$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,-3,4\pi ⟩ \\ ⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4t⟩ & =⟨0,-3,4\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t=0 \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t=-3 \\ 4t=4\pi .\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=\pi .$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(0,-3,4\pi )$ is at the tip of $r(\pi ).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,4⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,0,4⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,3,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -3 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-12i-9k \\  & =3(-4i-3k) \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =3\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{16+9} \\  & =3(5) \\  & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{15}{{5}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3}{{5}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186266125 :question/id #uuid "69bc0a02-5f33-5162-a5ed-5e7127e355db" :question/math-academy-id "q-131968"} {:db/id 17592186266126 :question/id #uuid 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\,{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩$ for $t>0$, use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(2,1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(2,1,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2,1,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t,\,{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩ & =⟨2,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2t=2 \\ {t}^{2}=1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,1,0)$ is at the tip of $r(1).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(1),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2t,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨2,2,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4i+2j+4k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+4+16} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{3}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186119948 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119518 :question/id #uuid "b17659af-7eb8-5922-a8b7-ab1e9dcfda08" :question/math-academy-id "e-12592"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ca07aabe-9fdd-5f28-b39f-1971c3591f86" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120301 :question/id #uuid "b869ac2c-0ead-501e-b8e6-38d06e66b5a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-34156"} {:db/id 17592186120302 :question/id #uuid "96d2a067-654d-55aa-b5c4-b48e4bab8c2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-34202"} {:db/id 17592186266128 :question/id #uuid "7eb005e4-b7c8-57e9-a9a3-c7cb18e5c9e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-132067"} {:db/id 17592186317438 :question/id #uuid "a8320061-9385-5e97-8a78-62a775ef29e2" :question/math-academy-id "q-34381"} {:db/id 17592186335742 :question/id #uuid "71c558ef-3d89-5d4c-b532-d4626f624683" :question/math-academy-id "q-64761"} {:db/id 17592186354512 :question/id #uuid "3f12f193-2cf6-5f7e-8614-5ffc56f6c861" :question/math-academy-id "q-86800"} {:db/id 17592186367415 :question/id #uuid "637c470e-0d8c-59d9-a6f9-8a2dca1476a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-132053"} {:db/id 17592186368615 :question/id #uuid "b07a41c9-a250-50fc-a699-42c7ad9094ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-64758"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve"} {:db/id 17592186119518 :question/id #uuid "b17659af-7eb8-5922-a8b7-ab1e9dcfda08" :question/math-academy-id "e-12592" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186119948 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ca07aabe-9fdd-5f28-b39f-1971c3591f86" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve"}] :question/problem "Using the cross product formula for curvature, find the curvature of $\mathbf r(t) = \langle 2t, 1+t^2\rangle$ as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the curvature $\kappa (t),$ we will use the following formula:

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩=⟨0,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\mathbf r''(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2,\,2t,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,2,\,0⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2t & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}2 & 2t \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \| = 4,
$$

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨2,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨2,\,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-2\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}}=\frac{2}{{2}^{3}}=\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186266128 :question/id #uuid "7eb005e4-b7c8-57e9-a9a3-c7cb18e5c9e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-132067" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119948 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3} .
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf r'(t) \|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,2,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4} \\  & =\sqrt{4({t}^{2}+1)} \\  & =2\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative $\mathbf{r}''(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)⟩=⟨2,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2t,2,0⟩\times ⟨2,0,0⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2t & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2t & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2t & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{4}{8({t}^{2}+1)^{3/2}}=\frac{1}{2({t}^{2}+1)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120156 :question/id #uuid "7f0173d8-1b20-5423-8c43-633f5b8b0c9b" :question/math-academy-id "q-165243" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119949 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨3,\,3t,\,{t}^{3}⟩$ for $t>0,$ use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩=⟨0,\,3,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(3)^{2}+(3{t}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9{t}^{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{9(1+{t}^{4})} \\  & =3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative ${r}^{″}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨0,\,3,\,3{t}^{2}⟩\times ⟨0,\,0,\,6t⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 3 & 3{t}^{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 6t\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 3{t}^{2} \\ 0 & 6t\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & 3{t}^{2} \\ 0 & 6t\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =18t\,i\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =|18t|=18t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $t>0$, we have $|t|=t.$
Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{18t}{{(3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}})}^{3}}=\frac{2t}{3(1+{t}^{4})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186354511 :question/id #uuid "bcaa2ffa-aada-5b80-a745-a2dbdb67535d" :question/math-academy-id "q-86799"} {:db/id 17592186368805 :question/id #uuid "b1e9fe5c-895e-5616-8f6f-1ceb3b387545" :topic/math-academy-id 1836} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120918 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121136 :tutorial/content "Recall that if the curve $\mathbf r(s)$ is parametrized by arc length $s,$ then the curvature of $\mathbf{r}$ is defined as

$$
\kappa(s) =  \left\| \dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf T}{\textrm{d}s}  \right\|.
$$

Moreover, if $\mathbf r(t)$ is parametrized by a general parameter $t,$ we have the following formula for the curvature:

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}
$$

where $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}$ is the unit tangent vector to the curve. 

It can be shown that the curvature of $\mathbf r(t)$ can also be found using the following cross product formula:

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}
$$

We'll derive this formula at the end of the lesson. For now, let's get some practice at applying it.

For example, suppose we would like to find the curvature of 
\[
\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle t, \: 1, \: t^2 \right\rangle
\]
at the point where [math]t = 0.[/math] 

First, we calculate [math]\mathbf r'(t),[/math] [math]\mathbf r'(0),[/math] and [math]\|\mathbf r'(0)\|\mathbin{:}[/math]

\begin{align*}
\mathbf r'(t) &= \left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t), \: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left(1\right), \: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left(t^2\right) \right\rangle \\[5pt]
&= \left \langle 1, \: 0, \: 2t \right \rangle \\[7pt]

\mathbf r'(0) &= \langle 1, 0, 0\rangle \\[7pt]

\| \mathbf r'(0) \| & = \sqrt{1^2 + 0^2 + 0^2} \\[3pt]
&= 1
\end{align*}

Now, we find [math]\mathbf r''(t)[/math] and [math]\mathbf r''(0)\mathbin{:}[/math]

\begin{align*}
\mathbf r''(t) & =  \left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(1), \: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left(0\right)  \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2t) \right\rangle \\[5pt]
&=\langle 0, 0, 2 \rangle \\[7pt]

\mathbf r''(0) &= \langle 0,0,2 \rangle
\end{align*}

Next, we compute the cross product and its magnitude:

\begin{align*}
\mathbf r'(0) \times \mathbf r''(0)  & = 
\begin{vmatrix}
  \mathbf i&	\mathbf j&	\mathbf k\\
  1& 		0&	 	0\\
  0& 		0& 		2
\end{vmatrix}\\[3pt]
&= \begin{array}{|cc|} 
		0 & 0 \\
		0 & 2
	\end{array} \, \mathbf{i} - 
\begin{array}{|cc|} 
		1 & 0 \\
		0 & 2
	\end{array} \, \mathbf{j} +
\begin{array}{|cc|} 
		1 & 0 \\
		0 & 0
	\end{array} \, \mathbf{k} \\[3pt]
&= -2\,\mathbf j \\[7pt]

\| \mathbf r'(0) \times \mathbf r''(0) \| &= 2
\end{align*}

Therefore, the curvature at [math]t=0[/math] is

\begin{align}
\kappa(0) &= \dfrac{\| \mathbf r'(0) \times \mathbf r''(0) \|}{\|\mathbf r'(0)\|^3} = \dfrac{2}{1^3} = 2.
\end{align}" :tutorial/id #uuid "699ec19c-b03f-5cc8-8096-613245aa4961" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7883 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3e7c32fc-b2a5-5b01-be28-7f715f065fb1" :step/math-academy-id 45439 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120919}} {:db/id 17592186120919 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119947 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119517 :question/id #uuid "f0213e01-520f-5b59-96d3-1d94a50deb82" :question/math-academy-id "e-12591"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "eddc00c0-eac2-5e79-84be-b90cc27eb054" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049132} {:db/id 17592186049196}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120325} {:db/id 17592186120496} {:db/id 17592186266124} {:db/id 17592186266125} {:db/id 17592186266126} {:db/id 17592186351506} {:db/id 17592186351507}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Curvature of a Curve at a Point"} :step/id #uuid "182c4b73-5dc9-53a4-835c-6d143dc732a6" :step/math-academy-id 45443 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120923}} {:db/id 17592186120920 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121137 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a plane curve $C$ that is parametrized by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle x(t), \: y(t) \rangle.
$$

At first glance, it looks as though the cross product curvature formula cannot be applied since cross products apply to three-dimensional vectors, whereas the given vector $\mathbf{r}(t)$ has only two dimensions.

\[
\kappa(t)=\dfrac{\|{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)}\times {\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime}(t)}\|}{\|{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)}\|^3}
\]

However, this curve can also be viewed as a curve in three-dimensional space that lies on the plane $z=0.$ In this case, $\mathbf{r}(t)$ can be considered as a vector-valued function with $z$-component equal to zero:

$$
\mathbf r(t)= \langle x(t), \: y(t), \: 0 \rangle
$$

As a result, the curvature $\kappa$ of our plane curve $C$ can be calculated using our cross product formula:

$$
\kappa(t)=\dfrac{\|{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)}\times {\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime}(t)}\|}{\|{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)}\|^3}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2ae1ba4c-311d-5298-8526-146a426bda14" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7884 :tutorial/title "Applying the Cross Product Formula to Plane Curves"} :step/id #uuid "405daa49-6e22-58fb-86e9-6e879a856c32" :step/math-academy-id 45446 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120921}} {:db/id 17592186120921 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119948 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119518 :question/id #uuid "b17659af-7eb8-5922-a8b7-ab1e9dcfda08" :question/math-academy-id "e-12592"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ca07aabe-9fdd-5f28-b39f-1971c3591f86" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120301} {:db/id 17592186120302} {:db/id 17592186266128} {:db/id 17592186317438} {:db/id 17592186335742} {:db/id 17592186354512} {:db/id 17592186367415} {:db/id 17592186368615}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve"} :step/id #uuid "bf0440fe-1ba1-52ce-be45-c99625d9108a" :step/math-academy-id 45447 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120922}} {:db/id 17592186120922 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121138 :tutorial/content "Recall that if the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ is parametrized by a general parameter $t,$ then the curvature of $\mathbf{r}$ is given by

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|},
$$

where $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}$ is the unit tangent vector to the curve. 

Here, $\mathbf r'(t)$ is a vector function and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|$ is a scalar function.
So, we differentiate $\mathbf T(t)$ by using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{'}(t) & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(T) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{{r}^{'}(t)}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{'}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{'}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}({r}^{'}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{'}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{''}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the cross product of a vector with itself equals $\mathbf{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\times {T}^{'}(t) & =\frac{{r}^{'}(t)}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}\times (\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{'}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{''}(t)) \\  & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{2}}\,({r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the magnitude of both sides and use the fact that $\mathbf T$ is a unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖T(t)\times {T}^{'}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)‖ \\ ‖T(t)‖\cdot ‖{T}^{'}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)‖ \\ 1\cdot ‖{T}^{'}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)‖ \\ ‖{T}^{'}(t)‖ & =\frac{‖{r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|} = \dfrac{\left\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \right\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f59936dc-ef8e-53d7-be8e-244d577dd658" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7885 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Cross Product Formula"} :step/id #uuid "1ca0f550-1726-5b03-9c0f-4d507624654b" :step/math-academy-id 45450} {:db/id 17592186120923 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119949 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119519 :question/id #uuid "0ad622cf-852f-5795-81ec-d147f050074e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12608"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3b61ddc7-b781-5a25-b499-1ea6f48abf36" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120156} {:db/id 17592186120497} {:db/id 17592186284537} {:db/id 17592186284538} {:db/id 17592186351508} {:db/id 17592186354509} {:db/id 17592186354511} {:db/id 17592186368805}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Curvature of a Curve at a General Point"} :step/id #uuid "390940d4-be4b-5226-9968-df737ec5e680" :step/math-academy-id 45507 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120920}}] :activity/title "Finding Curvature Using the Cross Product" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186120035} {:db/id 17592186120918 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121136 :tutorial/content "Recall that if the curve $\mathbf r(s)$ is parametrized by arc length $s,$ then the curvature of $\mathbf{r}$ is defined as

$$

Here, $\mathbf r'(t)$ is a vector function and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|$ is a scalar function.
So, we differentiate $\mathbf T(t)$ by using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{'}(t) & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(T) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{{r}^{'}(t)}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{'}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{'}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}({r}^{'}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{'}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{''}(t)\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\times {T}^{'}(t) & =\frac{{r}^{'}(t)}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}\times (\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖})\cdot {r}^{'}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{''}(t)) \\  & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{2}}\,({r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖T(t)\times {T}^{'}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)‖ \\ ‖T(t)‖\cdot ‖{T}^{'}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)‖ \\ 1\cdot ‖{T}^{'}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)‖ \\ ‖{T}^{'}(t)‖ & =\frac{‖{r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating $$

$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t),$ $\mathbf r'(1),$ and $\|\mathbf r'(1)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2,\,2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1,-2,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find $\mathbf r''(t)$ and $\mathbf r''(1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2),2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0,2⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,0,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4\,i-2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{20} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}}=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{{3}^{3}}=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{27}.\end{aligned}
